name: The Lord's Prayer
also_known_as: Our Father; Pater Noster; Otche Nash
used_at: Daily prayers; Divine Liturgy; Vespers; Matins; before meals
text_en: Our Father, Who art in heaven, hallowed be Thy name. Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread, and forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us; and lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from the evil one.
transliteration: Pater hēmōn ho en tois ouranois…
notes: The doxology ("For Thine is the kingdom…") is said by the priest, not the people, in the Byzantine rite — it is an exclamation, not part of the prayer.

name: The Trisagion
used_at: Trisagion Prayers; Divine Liturgy; daily prayers
text_en: Holy God, Holy Mighty, Holy Immortal, have mercy on us. (thrice)
transliteration: Hagios ho Theos, Hagios Ischyros, Hagios Athanatos, eleēson hēmas.
notes: Replaced at Pascha, Nativity, Theophany and Lazarus Saturday by "As many as have been baptized into Christ", and at the Exaltation of the Cross by "Before Thy Cross".

name: Glory Be
also_known_as: Lesser Doxology; Doxa Patri; Slava Otsu
used_at: Ends almost every sequence of prayers and psalms
text_en: Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen.
transliteration: Doxa Patri kai Huiō kai Hagiō Pneumati…
notes: The Byzantine form ends "unto ages of ages"; the Western "as it was in the beginning" clause is not used.

name: O Heavenly King
used_at: Opens most services and the daily prayer rule
origin: Byzantine; used as the opening invocation
text_en: O Heavenly King, the Comforter, the Spirit of Truth, Who art everywhere and fillest all things, Treasury of good things and Giver of life: come and abide in us, and cleanse us from every impurity, and save our souls, O Good One.
transliteration: Basileu ouranie, Paraklēte, to Pneuma tēs alētheias…
notes: Omitted from Pascha until Pentecost — during that period the Paschal Troparion takes its place. One of the few prayers addressed directly to the Holy Spirit.

name: The Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed
also_known_as: The Symbol of Faith; The Creed
origin: First Council of Nicaea 325; expanded at First Council of Constantinople 381
text_en: I believe in one God, the Father Almighty, Maker of heaven and earth, and of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, the Only-begotten, begotten of the Father before all ages; Light of Light, true God of true God, begotten, not made, of one essence with the Father, by Whom all things were made; Who for us men and for our salvation came down from heaven, and was incarnate of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, and became man; and was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, and suffered and was buried; and rose again on the third day according to the Scriptures; and ascended into heaven, and sitteth at the right hand of the Father; and shall come again with glory to judge the living and the dead, Whose kingdom shall have no end. And in the Holy Spirit, the Lord, the Giver of Life, Who proceedeth from the Father, Who with the Father and the Son together is worshipped and glorified, Who spake by the prophets. In one Holy, Catholic and Apostolic Church. I confess one baptism for the remission of sins. I look for the resurrection of the dead, and the life of the age to come. Amen.
transliteration: Pisteuō eis hena Theon, Patera Pantokratora…
notes: Recited WITHOUT the Filioque — "and the Son" — which is the central textual difference from the Western form and a defining point of Orthodox confession. Said in the first person singular ("I believe") in the Byzantine rite.

name: The Jesus Prayer
used_at: Private prayer; prayer rope; hesychast practice
origin: Desert Fathers; formalised in hesychast tradition, Mt Athos
text_en: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner.
transliteration: Kyrie Iēsou Christe, Huie tou Theou, eleēson me ton hamartōlon.
notes: Several lengths are in use; "a sinner" is sometimes omitted. Repeated on a prayer rope (komboskini / chotki) rather than counted aloud.

name: Lord, have mercy
used_at: Response to every petition of every litany
notes: Said 3, 12, 40 or 100 times depending on the litany. The single most frequently spoken line in Orthodox worship.

name: It Is Truly Meet
used_at: Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom; daily prayers
origin: 10th century; tradition attributes the first half to an angel on Mt Athos
text_en: It is truly meet to bless thee, O Theotokos, ever-blessed and most pure, and the Mother of our God. More honourable than the Cherubim, and beyond compare more glorious than the Seraphim, who without corruption gavest birth to God the Word: true Theotokos, we magnify thee.
transliteration: Axion estin hōs alēthōs makarizein se tēn Theotokon…
notes: Replaced by a seasonal hymn (the "Irmos of the Ninth Ode") on great feasts.

name: O Gladsome Light
used_at: Vespers, at the lighting of the lamps
origin: 2nd–3rd century — among the oldest hymns still in use
text_en: O Gladsome Light of the holy glory of the immortal Father, heavenly, holy, blessed Jesus Christ: now that we have come to the setting of the sun and behold the light of evening, we praise God: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. For meet it is at all times to worship Thee with voices of praise, O Son of God and Giver of life; therefore all the world doth glorify Thee.
notes: Cited by St Basil the Great in the 4th century as already ancient and of unknown authorship.

name: The Song of Symeon
used_at: Vespers; the Churching of a child
text_en: Lord, now lettest Thou Thy servant depart in peace, according to Thy word; for mine eyes have seen Thy salvation, which Thou hast prepared before the face of all people: a light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of Thy people Israel.
transliteration: Nyn apolyeis ton doulon sou, Despota…
notes: A canticle rather than a composed hymn — it is scripture sung as prayer.

name: Prayer of St Ephrem
origin: Attributed to St Ephrem the Syrian, 4th century
text_en: O Lord and Master of my life, take from me the spirit of sloth, despondency, lust of power and idle talk. But give rather the spirit of chastity, humility, patience and love to Thy servant. Yea, O Lord and King, grant me to see my own transgressions and not to judge my brother, for blessed art Thou unto ages of ages. Amen.
transliteration: Kyrie kai Despota tēs zōēs mou…
notes: Said with three full prostrations, then twelve bows, then a final prostration. Not used on Saturdays and Sundays of Lent, when prostrations are forbidden.

name: The Paschal Troparion
used_at: Paschal services; replaces O Heavenly King until Pentecost
text_en: Christ is risen from the dead, trampling down death by death, and upon those in the tombs bestowing life.
transliteration: Christos anestē ek nekrōn, thanatō thanaton patēsas…
notes: Sung constantly from Pascha to the Ascension. A troparion is a short hymn naming the theme of a feast — the hinge on which the day's whole service turns.

name: Prayer of the Publican
text_en: God, be merciful to me, a sinner.
transliteration: Ho Theos, hilasthēti moi tō hamartōlō.
notes: The scriptural root of the Jesus Prayer, and the model of Orthodox penitential prayer.

name: O Theotokos and Virgin, Rejoice
text_en: O Theotokos and Virgin, rejoice, Mary full of grace, the Lord is with thee. Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb, for thou hast borne the Saviour of our souls.
notes: The Byzantine counterpart of the Hail Mary, but with a different second half — it ends in proclamation rather than petition, and contains no request for intercession at the hour of death.

name: Prayer Before Communion
also_known_as: I Believe, O Lord, and I Confess
origin: Attributed to St John Chrysostom; the opening line is 1 Timothy 1:15
text_en: I believe, O Lord, and I confess that Thou art truly the Christ, the Son of the living God, Who camest into the world to save sinners, of whom I am first. I believe also that this is truly Thine own most pure Body, and that this is truly Thine own precious Blood. Therefore I pray Thee: have mercy upon me and forgive my transgressions, both voluntary and involuntary, of word and of deed, of knowledge and of ignorance; and make me worthy to partake without condemnation of Thine most pure Mysteries, unto remission of sins and life everlasting. Amen.
notes: One of several pre-communion prayers; the jurisdictions differ on how many are read.
